check_service_status.description: Check whether GDACS is answering, and how quickly. This is the one action that reports a problem as a value instead of failing the step, so a scheduled workflow can decide what to do about it - skip today's digest, wait, or say the data is stale rather than dying halfway through. Being rate limited is reported separately from being down.

count_disasters.description: Count the disasters in a window, split by hazard and by alert level, without fetching any of them. One small answer however big the number, which makes it the cheap way for a schedule to ask 'was there anything serious?' before doing the expensive part - and the way to size a search before running it. There is deliberately no country here: GDACS can only narrow a count by matching a country's name as text, which would count Nigeria's floods as Niger's, and a wrong total is worse than none. Search disasters filters countries exactly and reports how many it found.

find_disasters_affecting_place.description: Find the disasters whose affected area covers a place - an office, a warehouse, a supplier, a customer's address - nearest first, each with how far away its centre is and in which direction. GDACS does the covering test itself against the real mapped shapes: a flood's inundated area, an earthquake's shaking contours, a cyclone's wind swath. That is the difference between 'an earthquake happened 200 km away' and 'this site is inside the strong-shaking zone'. 'is_affected' is the single true or false to branch on. Testing a place against every mapped shape is real work, so this one takes a few seconds where the others take under one.

description: Watch the world's natural disasters through GDACS, the Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System run by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre and the United Nations. It monitors earthquakes, tropical cyclones, floods, volcanoes, wildfires and droughts worldwide and rates each one green, orange or red for the humanitarian impact it expects - so a workflow can tell a magnitude 7 under an empty ocean from a magnitude 6 under a city. See what is happening right now, search the archive by hazard, severity, dates and country, check whether a specific address sits inside a disaster's mapped area, read the details and the news coverage, measure how far an event reaches, and look up a country's counted disaster history back to 1900. No API key, no sign-up and no quota.
